title: In skeptical Ottawa, ghost hunting can be a tough sell, purveyors of the paranormal say
excerpt: Psychic entertainers, ghost hunters and everyday residents share their experiences of the paranormal scene in Ottawa.
content:
Some say Ottawa is a ghost town, though for a different reason than you may think.

Ghost hunters, psychics and some more mainstream residents say they have had experiences with the supernatural in the capital. They are not alone as about 44 per cent of Canadians surveyed says they believe in the paranormal, according to a 2025 poll done for the publication, The Conversation.

Perhaps that’s why some take part in ghostly tourism in the capital with companies such as the The Haunted Walk, which offers several tours in the city and in Kingston and Toronto. But one of its better known tours of the Saintlo Ottawa Jail Hostel ended in 2023 at the request of the hostel.

So it’s not all good news for the paranormal, says Ariel Waller who is responsible for guest experiences at the Saintlo Ottawa Jail Hostel. Even with a more than 25-year tradition of sharing ghost stories, people “have moved away from ghost tourism in recent years,” Waller told Capital Current.

As Halloween draws near, Jaymes White, a psychic entertainer with a decade of experience hosting séances to contact spirits, agrees, saying Ottawa is “not as accepting to the paranormal as other cities.”

But despite what he calls a “tough market” for ghost entertainment, scary stories linger in the some corners.

“The old (Saintlo) youth hostel, there’s always something happening there,” said John Buffam, a ghost hunter who helped found Bytown Paranormal in 2010. 

The team, which has more than 27,000 Facebook followers, has investigated the hostel “five or six times,” Buffam said. 

He said in an early investigation, a member of the team heard a haunting voice from a cell saying, “You don’t belong here.”

Buffam said he believes ghost hunting in Ottawa is harder because it’s “a government city,” and government agencies such as Parks Canada do not always grant permission to investigate reportedly haunted sites, such as Laurier House. 

Martin Lee, another ghost hunter on the team, said “business” considerations also factor in to whether places such as the Bytown Museum and Fairmont Château Laurier allow paranormal investigations.

Psychic entertainer White talked about stories from Château Laurier, where he said the ghost of its original builder, Charles Melville Hays, may lurk. Hays died when the Titanic sank before the hotel’s opening in 1912.

Hotel management declined comment on the issue of ghosts.

These stories are the reason White said he came back to the city to host the Elmvale Ward Séance, after a decade of séances in Toronto that he said gathered more than 25,000 participants.

The former “District Hospital” at 2935 Conroy Rd. is the site for his séances this month and next.

To provoke conversations with spirits, White brought his ghost hunting equipment and various ‘haunted’ items from his collection of more than 500 items to Ottawa. 

From a fan of his work in Italy, for example, he says, he received a “REM-Pod,” which he said “creates its own electromagnetic field” using its telescopic antenna, triggering a sound when it detects disturbances.

White previously tested the device on a taxidermy bear he received from Montreal, which he said caused a beeping. He said the bear originally resided in a museum that closed 15 years ago, and when it changed hands to its new owners, he said, they had reportedly spotted its head move.

Buffam and Lee of Bytown Paranormal said they approach paranormal investigations “scientifically” and “pragmatically.”

Lee said they use ghost-hunting equipment “to try to disprove that [something] is haunted first. Unless we have concrete evidence that it’s a haunting, we just can’t assume.” 

Not all of Ottawa’s alleged experiences with ghosts are in more well-known locations. 

Beneath the ByWard Market sits a cellar built in 1875, now home to Apothecary Cocktail Lounge, where patrons can enjoy a spirit — and possibly a ghost too. 

Bartender Phill Macleod says during his time at Apothecary he’s had experiences he felt were “paranormal.”

“It’s mostly just weird stuff happening that no one can explain, like noises or seeing things moving, and nobody’s there,” he said. 

Macleod said the most creepy part of the historic building is the “heartbeat” thudding that the radiator makes while he is closing the bar late at night. 

Another server of two and a half years, Danielle Lazare, said she “was ignoring everyone, and didn’t believe in the rumours about ghosts” until she experienced something strange herself. 

Lazare said that one night, when resupplying toilet paper from upstairs, she went into the supply room and spotted a “weird shadow” that resembled her friend.

Suddenly, she said, the door shut behind her, and when she went to confront her friend afterwards, he said he had never left the basement. 

“I don’t know if it’s actually haunted or if there’s like crazy stuff going on here, but it’s definitely odd, definitely odd,” she said.
